title: Forwarded HTTP Extension
summary: Defines the Forwarded HTTP header field, which lets proxies pass along information that would otherwise be lost, such as the original client IP address. It standardizes what was done with the informal X-Forwarded-For style headers. It also gives guidelines for administrators who want to anonymize request origins.

eli5.summary: When a letter passes through several post offices, each one can write on it who sent it first. This standard header does that for web requests so the final server knows the original sender.

questions: how do proxies pass client ip
how do proxies pass the client ip
what does the for parameter mean
subtitle: A standard HTTP header that lets proxies tell the next server who originally made the request.

tldr.problem: When a proxy sits between a client and a web server, the server sees the proxy's address instead of the client's, and other details of the original request are lost or changed.
tldr.mechanism: The optional Forwarded header lists parameter pairs (by, for, host, proto) that each proxy can add, so the server can see the original client address, the proxy interface, the original Host value and the protocol used.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the informal X-Forwarded-* headers with one standard field, but it exposes sensitive information, so it should be off by default and the data cannot be trusted without trusted proxies.

today: RFC 7239 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It remains the definition of the Forwarded header field.

sections.title: Why Proxies Lose Information
sections.content:
Many HTTP requests pass through proxies the user never chose. A company may run a proxy for load balancing or crypto offload, or an organization may run one to cache resources. Either way, the request appears to come from the proxy's IP address, and the proxy may change other details of the original request.

That loss hurts servers that need the client's address for diagnostics (logging, troubleshooting, statistics), access control (allow-lists of client addresses) and abuse management. Reverse proxies hide information in the same way.

Before this RFC, people used non-standard fields such as X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-By and X-Forwarded-Proto. RFC 7239 standardizes a single Forwarded field. Because everything sits in one field, a server can tell which pieces of information belong together, as long as the proxies are trusted. The field is optional, so proxies meant to provide privacy do not have to implement it.
sections.eli5: A helper who carries your message to someone else puts their own name on it, and the receiver forgets who you were. This header is a note that keeps your name on the message.

sections.title: The Forwarded Header Field
sections.content:
Forwarded is an optional header field for requests only; it must not be used in responses. It holds a list of elements. The first element holds information added by the first proxy that uses the field, and each later element comes from the next proxy. Inside one element, parameter-identifier pairs are joined by an equals sign and separated by semicolons. A parameter MUST NOT appear more than once per element, and parameter names are case-insensitive.

Values are either a token or a quoted-string. Since : and [ ] are not valid in a token, IPv6 addresses (and any address with a port) are written as quoted strings.

  • Forwarded: for="_gazonk"
  • Forwarded: for=192.0.2.60;proto=http;by=203.0.113.43
  • Forwarded: for=192.0.2.43, for=198.51.100.17

A proxy can add its element by appending to the last existing Forwarded field after a comma, or by adding a new field at the end of the header block. A proxy MAY remove all Forwarded fields, but it MUST make sure the correct field is updated when there are several. Because the data is sensitive, the field should be turned off by default, and each parameter should be configured individually.
sections.eli5: It is a list where each helper adds one line about who handed the message to them. Each line is made of small labels like "from" and "by", each with a value.

sections.title: The Four Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 7239 defines four parameters:

  • by identifies the user-agent facing interface of the proxy, the interface where the request came in. Reverse proxies mostly add it for the backend server, and it can be useful on a multihomed proxy.
  • for identifies the node making the request to the proxy. In a full chain the first for is the original client, followed by each later proxy. The last proxy is not listed in for, since its address is already the remote address at the transport layer.
  • host carries the original Host request header value as the proxy received it, which helps when a reverse proxy rewrites Host to an internal name.
  • proto says which protocol was used to make the request, typically http or https. An origin server behind a crypto-offloading proxy can use it to rewrite URLs to match what the client used.

For by and for, the default configuration SHOULD use an obfuscated identifier. A real IP address (and possibly a port) MAY be used if the receiving server needs address-based behavior, and unknown is a third option. Extension parameters are allowed and SHOULD be registered.
sections.eli5: There are four labels: who came in (for), which door they came through (by), what address they asked for (host) and whether they used the plain or the locked door (proto).

sections.title: Node Identifiers
sections.content:
The value of by and for is a node identifier: a name part with an optional port. The name part is one of three things: an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address in square brackets, the word unknown, or an obfuscated identifier.

unknown is for when a proxy does not know the preceding entity but still wants to signal that forwarding happened, for example a proxy process that generates an outgoing request without direct access to the incoming TCP socket.

An obfuscated identifier lets the operator keep internal addresses secret while still allowing tracing and debugging. It MUST start with an underscore and may contain only letters, digits and a dot, an underscore and a hyphen. Unless a server needs static identifiers, they SHOULD be randomly generated for each request, and if they must persist, they SHOULD NOT persist longer than client IP addresses. The port can also be obfuscated in the same way. IPv6 addresses SHOULD follow the text representation recommendations of RFC 5952.

Any nodename with a port, and any IPv6 address, MUST be quoted, for example "[2001:db8:cafe::17]:47011".
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a real house address, a helper can write a secret nickname like _hidden. Anyone can follow the trail, but nobody learns where the house is.

sections.title: Using It in Practice
sections.content:
An HTTP list may have whitespace between elements and may be split over several header fields, so for=192.0.2.43,for=unknown is equivalent to the same elements written on separate lines. A directly forwarded request should keep and possibly extend the field. If one incoming request causes several outbound requests, the proxy has to judge whether each is a direct consequence of the incoming one; if it is not, the field should not be preserved.

Via has a similar purpose but only describes the proxy itself, not the client connecting to it, and since Via is already widely deployed its format could not be changed. The two fields cannot be reliably combined because some proxies update one, the other or both.

For transition, a proxy that receives X-Forwarded-* fields is encouraged to convert them where that makes sense. For example, X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.43, 2001:db8:cafe::17 becomes Forwarded: for=192.0.2.43, for="[2001:db8:cafe::17]". If several X-Forwarded fields coexist, the order they were added in cannot be known, so conversion may be impossible.
sections.eli5: If an old-style note and a new-style note both exist, a helper can copy the old note onto the new form, but only if they can tell which line was written first.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The field cannot be relied on to be correct. Any node on the path, including the client, can change it by mistake or on purpose. Whitelisting trusted proxies helps, but the chain of addresses listed before the request reached the trusted proxy still cannot be trusted, and unless the link between proxies and the endpoint is secured, an attacker with network access can change the data.

The field can also reveal internal network structure. Remedies are obfuscated identifiers, stopping internal nodes from updating it, or having an egress proxy remove entries. Origin servers and intermediaries should never copy it into responses, and hosting environments need care with TRACE, where the field would appear in the response body.

A client IP address can identify a client, its operator and roughly where it is. If a request contains header fields that specifically ask for privacy, a proxy SHOULD NOT use Forwarded or pass private information such as IP addresses to the next hop. The field itself, even without a unique client identifier, may make fingerprinting easier by revealing the proxy chain.
sections.eli5: Anyone along the way could scribble a fake name on the note, and the note can tell strangers where your house is. So keep it off unless you need it and trust the helpers.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The Forwarded header field is added to the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry as a standard field. RFC 7239 also creates the HTTP Forwarded Parameters registry, with by, for, host and proto as the initial entries. New parameters are assigned by IETF Review, must fit the forwarded-pair syntax, and their security and privacy implications should be thoroughly documented.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed labels. New labels can be added only after a careful review.
